abstract: Exchange-only quantum computing benefits from high fidelity and straightforward control afforded by the exchange interaction. However, independently controllable qubits must be encoded into subsystems of at least three electron spins, restricting computation to only a fraction of the available spin Hilbert space. The remaining states are treated as leakage and used only transiently in gate sequences. By contrast, a quantitative, system-wide measure of exchange-only performance can exploit the full available Hilbert space, including states conventionally treated as leakage. Here, we apply this approach to arrays of up to 48 electron spins, accessing a total-spin-zero Hilbert space with dimension exceeding $2^{40}$. Measurements of out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) reveal rich scrambling dynamics and demonstrate access to regimes relevant to quantum computational advantage. Using generalized forms of cross-entropy and mirror randomized benchmarking, we also assess the aggregate performance of the full exchange-only system per fundamental two-body interaction: the two-spin exchange. We obtain an effective system-level error of $3 \times 10^{-4}$ per exchange, incorporating the complete experimental control sequence and all associated noise sources. This value is up to an order of magnitude lower than those reported from comparable benchmarks on other platforms at the time of writing.
summary: This work benchmarks quantum computation performance using only exchange interactions on large arrays of electron spins. By measuring performance across the entire accessible Hilbert space, the authors report a very low system-level error rate. This demonstrates a scalable and high-fidelity method for controlling complex quantum many-body systems using solid-state spin qubits.
main_problem: The paper benchmarks quantum control using only exchange interactions on a large spin system, aiming to utilize the entire available Hilbert space rather than restricting to smaller, conventionally treated subspaces.
main_result: The authors achieved an effective system-level error of $3 	imes 10^{-4}$ per exchange, which is reported to be up to an order of magnitude lower than comparable benchmarks on other platforms.
method: Performance is assessed using Out-of-Time-Order Correlators (OTOCs) to study scrambling dynamics, and generalized forms of cross-entropy and mirror randomized benchmarking (MRB) to quantify aggregate error.
model_or_system: The system consists of arrays of up to 48 electron spins (quantum dots) whose evolution is governed solely by voltage-controlled spin-spin exchange interactions, operating within the total-spin-zero Hilbert space.
key_observables: Effective system-level error ($\epsilon_F$), scrambling dynamics (via OTOCs), fidelity, and purity.
important_parameters: System size up to 48 spins; total-spin-zero Hilbert space dimension exceeding $2^{40}$; error rate of $3 	imes 10^{-4}$ per exchange.
main_assumptions: The control relies on $S$-conserving exchange operations, and the approach assumes the ability to measure performance across the full Hilbert space, treating previously 'leakage' states as usable.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the scaling of the accessible Hilbert space, schematics of the QPU chip, and benchmarking procedures (XEB, RB, MRB) used to measure error rates.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the concept of full Hilbert space benchmarking for exchange-only control, details the application to large spin arrays, presents measurements using OTOCs and randomized benchmarking techniques, and concludes with the reported low error rates.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, high-fidelity benchmark for scaling quantum computation using only native, local interactions (exchange), which is highly relevant for solid-state quantum computing architectures.
